subject: Vocabulary
description: Same-sound, different-spelling-and-meaning words — high-hit pairs in SSC/Bank exams

options.option_text: Has the same spelling but different meanings
Sounds the same as another word but has a different spelling and meaning
Means the opposite of another word
Is borrowed from a foreign language

questions.explanation: Homophone (Greek: 'same sound') — words with identical pronunciation but different spelling AND meaning, e.g., 'their / there / they're', 'flower / flour'. Don't confuse with: homograph (same spelling, possibly different pronunciation, e.g. 'lead' the metal vs 'lead' to guide); homonym (same spelling AND same pronunciation but different meanings, e.g. 'bank' the river-side vs 'bank' the institution); synonyms (different words, similar meaning); antonyms (opposites).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correctly used homophone: 'The new policy will _____ the morale of the staff.'

options.option_text: boost
boast
bust
boost'd

questions.explanation: BOOST = increase / lift up. BOAST = brag, talk proudly. BUST = break or a sculpted upper body. The morale gets BOOSTED (raised), not boasted. Common homophone-style trap pair tested in Bank PO papers. Tip: 'oo' in BOOST sounds like the U-shape lifting up.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'STATIONARY' and 'STATIONERY' differ in meaning. Which sentence uses the correct word?

options.option_text: I bought new pens from the stationary shop.
The car remained stationary at the red light.
Please order more stationary for the office.
The bicycle is parked in stationery.

questions.explanation: STATIONARY (with -ARY) = NOT moving — adjective. 'The car remained stationary' ✓. STATIONERY (with -ERY) = writing materials (paper, pens, envelopes) — noun. Mnemonic: stationERY has 'E' for envelope. Stationary cars stay (also has 'a').
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct homophone: 'The committee will _____ the awards on Friday.'

options.option_text: compliment
complement
confer
consensus

questions.explanation: CONFER = to grant or bestow (formal sense, used for awards/honours). COMPLIMENT = praise (verb/noun). COMPLEMENT = something that completes (e.g., 'wine is a good complement to the meal'). CONSENSUS = general agreement. Mnemonic: COMPLIment with an 'I' for 'I praise you'; COMPLEment with an 'E' for 'completes an Ensemble'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Identify the correct homophone in: 'The _____ of his speech was on educational reform.'

options.option_text: principal
principle
principles'
principalship

questions.explanation: PRINCIPLE = a fundamental belief, rule or law (noun). 'The principle of his speech' = the underlying main idea. PRINCIPAL = head of a school (noun) OR main / most important (adjective). Mnemonic: principal ends in '-pal' — your school principal is your pal. principle ends in '-ple' — like a 'rule'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'AFFECT' is to 'EFFECT' as 'PRACTICE' is to 'PRACTISE'. Which best describes the rule?

options.option_text: Both pairs are interchangeable
First in each pair is verb in American English; differs in British English
First is always noun; second is always verb in both dialects
There is no rule — it is purely random

questions.explanation: British English: PRACTICE (noun) vs PRACTISE (verb). 'Cricket practice' — the noun. 'I will practise daily' — the verb. American English uses PRACTICE for both. AFFECT (verb, to influence) vs EFFECT (noun, the result; also rare verb meaning to bring about) — distinction holds in both dialects. Memory: 'Affect = Action' (verb), 'Effect = End-result' (noun).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct word from the pair 'COUNCIL / COUNSEL'?

options.option_text: He sought legal council before signing.
She offered me wise counsel about the job change.
The county counsel meeting begins at 5 PM.
Members of the city counsel were sworn in.

questions.explanation: COUNSEL (n./v.) = advice / to advise (also a lawyer is 'counsel'). 'She offered wise counsel' ✓. COUNCIL (n.) = a deliberative body / committee. 'City Council', 'Security Council'. Mnemonic: counCIL has 'CIL' for ChIef governing body, while counSEL has 'SEL' for adviSEr. Note: 'counsellor' (UK) and 'counselor' (US) refer to a person who gives advice; 'councillor' (UK) / 'councilor' (US) sits on a council.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences correctly uses a word from the homophone pair 'PREY / PRAY'?

options.option_text: The hawk circled above, waiting to swoop down on its pray below.
Fraudsters often pray on the financial desperation of the elderly.
The hawk circled above, waiting to swoop down on its prey below.
She stopped at the roadside temple to prey for her family's wellbeing.

questions.explanation: 'Prey' (noun/verb) refers to an animal hunted by another, or to victimise; 'pray' means to offer worship or petition. Option C correctly uses 'prey' in a hunting context. Option A swaps 'pray' into the hunting context; Option B wrongly uses 'pray' where 'prey on' (to exploit) is needed; Option D uses 'prey' in a worship context where 'pray' is correct.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence that correctly uses a word from the homophone pair 'HOARD / HORDE'.

options.option_text: A horde of old coins and manuscripts was discovered in the ancient cellar.
A hoard of excited supporters gathered outside the stadium before the match.
The smuggler kept a large hoard of contraband goods hidden in the godown.
The smuggler kept a large horde of contraband goods hidden in the godown.

questions.explanation: 'Hoard' means a secretly stored stock of valuables; 'horde' means a large unruly crowd or group. Option C correctly uses 'hoard' for stored contraband. Option D places 'horde' in the identical sentence — a classic swap trap. Options A and B reverse the pair entirely, misapplying 'horde' to objects and 'hoard' to a crowd.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a word from the homophone pair 'ELICIT / ILLICIT'?

options.option_text: The officer struggled to illicit a proper response during the interrogation session.
The CBI seized several elicit weapons during the coordinated raids across the state.
The officer managed to elicit a full confession from the suspect under questioning.
The court confirmed that the elicit transactions had violated all banking regulations.

questions.explanation: 'Elicit' is a verb meaning to draw out or evoke; 'illicit' is an adjective meaning unlawful or forbidden. Option C correctly uses 'elicit' as a verb. Option A wrongly treats 'illicit' as a verb — a very common error. Options B and D misuse 'elicit' as an adjective modifying weapons and transactions, where 'illicit' (illegal) is required.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that correctly uses a word from the homophone pair 'FLAIR / FLARE'.

options.option_text: The veteran pilot had an extraordinary flare for navigating high-altitude terrain.
The rescue team launched a distress flair that was spotted from the hilltop post.
The young dancer showed a natural flair for classical Bharatanatyam performances.
The diplomat had a special flare for resolving sensitive international border disputes.

questions.explanation: 'Flair' means a natural talent or aptitude; 'flare' means a sudden burst of light or flame, or to widen outward. Option C correctly uses 'flair' for innate talent. Options A and D misuse 'flare' in contexts requiring talent ('flair'); Option B misuses 'flair' in a light-signal context where 'flare' is the correct word.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences correctly uses a word from the pair 'COMPLEMENT / COMPLIMENT'?

options.option_text: The new irrigation scheme will compliment the existing water conservation policy.
The senior officer paid a complement to the team for their flood relief efforts.
The new irrigation scheme will complement the existing water conservation policy.
The minister's complements to the young scientists inspired the entire gathering.

questions.explanation: 'Complement' means something that completes or enhances another; 'compliment' means an expression of praise. Option C correctly uses 'complement' — the scheme enhances the policy. Option A misuses 'compliment' (praise) where enhancement is meant; Option B misuses 'complement' where a verbal tribute ('compliment') is needed; Option D uses 'complements' where 'compliments' is required.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'DISCRETE' (not 'DISCREET') in the appropriate context?

options.option_text: The statistical model treated income as a discrete variable with fixed, separate values.
The IAS officer handled the sensitive land dispute in a discrete and tactful manner.
The ambassador's discrete conversations were vital to the success of the peace talks.
The auditor conducted discrete inquiries to avoid alerting the management beforehand.

questions.explanation: 'Discrete' means individually separate and distinct — a technical term in mathematics and statistics for non-continuous variables. 'Discreet' means careful and circumspect in behaviour. Only Option A demands 'discrete' (separate categories in a statistical model). Options B, C, and D all describe tactful or cautious behaviour, where 'discreet' is required — candidates who confuse the spelling routinely pick these.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a word from the homophone pair 'EMINENT / IMMINENT'?

options.option_text: The eminent landfall of Cyclone Biparjoy prompted mass evacuation of coastal villages.
The imminent historian delivered a keynote lecture on the Mauryan Empire at Nalanda.
The landfall of Cyclone Biparjoy was declared imminent by the meteorological department.
The eminent danger posed by rising floodwaters compelled the district collector to act.

questions.explanation: 'Imminent' means about to happen very soon; 'eminent' means famous, distinguished, or outstanding. Option C correctly uses 'imminent' for a cyclone's approaching landfall. Option A swaps 'eminent' into an impending-event context; Option B absurdly describes a historian as 'imminent'; Option D is the classic exam trap — 'eminent danger' sounds natural but is wrong; the correct phrase is 'imminent danger'.
